title: No Collarbones at All: A Pre-Surgery X-Ray Exposed a 78-Year-Old Laborer's Lifelong Secret
text:
No Collarbones at All: A Pre-Surgery X-Ray Exposed a 78-Year-Old Laborer's Lifelong Secret
A 78-year-old man in rural Uganda went to the hospital to fix a hernia. A routine chest X-ray taken before the operation turned up something far stranger: he had no collarbones at all. He had spent most of his working life doing manual labor and told doctors his shoulders had "always been this way."
Surgeons at Kampala International University Western Campus in Ishaka, Uganda, and the Université Catholique du Graben in the Democratic Republic of Congo described the case on August 10, 2026, in the International Medical Case Reports Journal. Complete absence of both collarbones, called bilateral clavicular agenesis, is extremely rare and is usually caught in childhood.
A Hernia Visit with an Unexpected Finding
The man came in with a reducible swelling in his left groin that had been growing for two years and caused mild, dull pain. He had undergone a repair of the same hernia at another facility a decade earlier. His other major condition was high blood pressure, controlled for more than 30 years with amlodipine and losartan.
The anomaly surfaced when doctors examined his chest and shoulders. Both shoulders drooped, and his shoulder girdle was so loose that he could nearly bring his shoulders together in front of his chest. He reported no pain, weakness, or limitation in his arms.
The standard chest X-ray ordered for older surgical patients confirmed it. His heart and lungs looked normal, but there was no trace of either collarbone. His chest had a somewhat bell-shaped contour, while his ribs and other visible bones appeared intact.
The Usual Explanation Did Not Quite Fit
Missing collarbones are best known as a hallmark of cleidocranial dysplasia, a genetic condition that affects bones and teeth. According to MedlinePlus Genetics, it occurs in about one in a million people worldwide and is usually caused by changes in the RUNX2 gene, which helps direct bone formation. In about 30% of people with the condition, no RUNX2 change is found. Some also have hearing loss or frequent sinus and ear infections.
The disorder typically shows itself early. Children often have soft spots in the skull that close late, extra or unerupted teeth, and an unusual ability to bring their shoulders forward, signs the authors say usually prompt a pediatric workup. Late diagnoses do happen; a 2022 report described cleidocranial dysplasia that was found incidentally and diagnosed late.
This man had none of the skull or facial features. His face was symmetrical, his skull showed no persistent defects, and a basic look inside his mouth found adult teeth without obvious retained baby teeth or severe misalignment. The authors concluded he had either a highly localized form of the genetic condition or an even rarer isolated absence of the collarbones. No reliable prevalence data exist for the isolated form, they note.
The collarbone is also unusual developmentally. It is the first bone to begin hardening in the embryo, around the fifth or sixth week of pregnancy, and the last to finish, the authors wrote.
Muscles Took Over the Collarbone's Job
The collarbone is the only bony strut linking the arm to the trunk. It positions the shoulder and shields nerves and blood vessels underneath. So how did this man lift, carry, and labor for decades without it?
The authors point to the surrounding muscles. Without the bony brace, the trapezius, serratus anterior, sternocleidomastoid, and pectoralis major appear to adapt enough to steady the shoulder for lifting and carrying loads. The case, they argue, supports the idea that the collarbone improves leverage but is not strictly essential for daily activities or hard physical work, as long as those muscles compensate.
The finding still mattered in the operating room. Without collarbones, landmarks doctors use to place central venous catheters are altered, which could raise the risk of a punctured lung or blood vessel. Related skeletal conditions can also involve narrow airways that complicate anesthesia. Here, surgeons repaired the hernia under spinal anesthesia with no airway or breathing problems, and he recovered uneventfully.
Why Doctors Chose to Leave It Alone
The team decided no orthopedic or genetic intervention was needed, citing his age, lack of symptoms, and excellent adaptation. The authors framed this as a lesson in clinical restraint: a dramatic X-ray finding in a healthy older adult does not have to trigger a cascade of tests and treatments.
Resources also shaped the workup. In high-income settings, genetic testing for RUNX2 changes would be standard, and it can help assess related risks such as bone density loss or hearing problems. In rural Uganda, the authors note, such tests often cost more than a patient's annual income.
That leaves real gaps. Genetic sequencing, a dental X-ray, a dental specialist consultation and detailed skull CT were not available, so a mild genetic variant or subtle dental signs cannot be ruled out. As a single case, the report, indexed in PubMed, cannot say how often adults live unaware of the condition.
For readers, the practical points are modest. Cleidocranial dysplasia is passed down in an autosomal dominant pattern and affects boys and girls equally, and MedlinePlus recommends genetic counseling for people with a personal or family history who are planning to have children. Anyone heading into surgery should tell the care team about known skeletal differences.
Key Questions Answered
What did doctors find?
A chest X-ray before hernia surgery showed that a 78-year-old man had no collarbones on either side.
How did he manage without collarbones?
He reported no limitations during a lifetime of manual labor. The authors believe his shoulder and neck muscles compensated.
What usually causes missing collarbones?
Most often, cleidocranial dysplasia, a rare genetic condition usually tied to the RUNX2 gene that also affects the skull and teeth.
Did he have that condition?
It is unclear. He lacked the typical skull and dental features, and genetic testing was not available.
Did the finding affect his surgery?
His hernia was repaired under spinal anesthesia without airway or breathing problems, and he recovered uneventfully.
Does the condition need treatment?
Not in his case. Doctors chose no orthopedic or genetic intervention because he had no symptoms and functioned well.
